title: Any feeling, turned to Krishna
hook: a king stops the story to ask how the gopis' love could set them free
carry: any feeling, turned to Krishna, reaches him
tomorrow: he vanished. how do the gopis find him again?

segments.voice: Yesterday: the flute on the full-moon night. The gopis left the milk on the fire and went just as they were, the tradition's own picture of bhakti.

Before the dance, a king interrupts. In the Bhagavata, the sage Shuka is telling this story to King Parikshit, who has just heard about the women running into the forest at night. He stops the story. These women, he says, knew Krishna as a beloved, not as the highest truth. Their minds were full of him the way a lover's mind is full. How could that set them free? It's a fair question, and the text answers it before going one step further.
screen: `A KING INTERRUPTS.` → `THEY KNEW HIM AS A BELOVED.` → `HOW COULD THAT SET THEM FREE?`

segments.voice: Shuka's answer goes back to an earlier story: Shishupala, a king who hated Krishna, spent his life thinking of him in rage, and still reached him in the end. If hatred fixed on him could do that, Shuka says, then whoever turns the whole mind toward him, in desire or anger, fear, affection, kinship or friendship, becomes absorbed in him. What matters is where the mind is pointed. That's a big idea in Hindu bhakti: God isn't reached only through calm, correct feelings. Whatever you truly feel, turned wholly toward him, becomes the road. Only then does the story go on. The women arrive, out of breath, and Krishna greets them like a polite host. Then he tells them to go home. The night is dark, the forest full of animals, your families will be looking for you, your place is with them. It's a test, and it lands hard. The gopis stand with eyes down, scratching the ground with their toes, crying. Then they answer. Their hearts were taken by him, they say, and their feet won't carry them back. They came not for a household but for him. Krishna smiles, stays, and the night of play in the forest begins. As he honors them, the women grow proud, each one sure she is the most favored woman in the world. At that moment, the text says, Krishna vanishes. Some devotional teachers read the whole episode as the soul's longing for God, told in the language of human love; Parikshit's question is the text's own reminder to read it that way.
screen: `ANY FEELING, TURNED TO HIM.` · `GO HOME, HE SAYS.` · `OUR FEET WON'T CARRY US BACK.` · then, large: `PRIDE, AND HE VANISHES.`

segments.voice: Let the breath settle and watch where your mind points on its own: a person, a worry, a plan. Each time you catch it, name the direction quietly, toward work, toward someone, toward tomorrow, and come back to the breath. If you pray, turn your mind toward God, or toward Krishna, for one breath, then simply watch again.
Rasa lila. Krishna's night of dance and play with the gopis, which the Bhagavata frames as a story about where the whole mind is turned.
Your line: any feeling, turned to Krishna, reaches him. Tomorrow: he vanished, so how do they find him? Day nine hundred, done.

howItsDone: The rasa lila chapters of the Bhagavata are recited at katha and sung by Krishna devotees, and danced in the Ras Lila performances of Vrindavan; many temples keep the autumn full moon, Sharad Purnima, as the night of the rasa, and teachers in the devotional traditions present it as a picture of the soul's love for God.

notes: The index title promises 'the Keeper's framing'. This script uses only the frame the Bhagavata itself gives (Parikshit's question and Shuka's answer in 10.29); the Hindu path's Keeper should supply or approve the framing before release. The script never mentions a Keeper in the voice.

All paraphrase. Confirm against Bhagavata 10.29: Parikshit's question (gopis knew him as a lover, not as Brahman); Shuka's answer citing Shishupala and the list (desire, anger, fear, affection, kinship, friendship); Krishna's speech sending them home; the gopis scratching the ground with their toes and their reply; their pride and his vanishing at the chapter's end.
The adult and erotic elements of the rasa lila are kept implicit ('the night of play'). A Keeper should judge the level for a general audience.
'Devotional teachers in this tradition read the whole episode as the soul's longing for God' is a general claim; a Keeper may want to name a school or soften.
